comment: THE CREDENTIAL SHAPES THIS STACK ACTUALLY HANDLES, as reviewed data for tools/check-secrets.mjs (chain step 4).

WHY A SECOND SCANNER EXISTS. gitleaks is the deep one and it is not always there: lefthook prints `SKIP secrets scan` when the binary is absent, and .github/workflows/gitleaks.yml only runs after a PUSH. So on any machine without gitleaks a turn could end green with a service-role key in a tracked file, and the first thing that would notice is a workflow running after the bytes are already in the remote. This gate is zero-dependency node, runs inside the chain, and is therefore present on every machine and in every turn.

DELIBERATELY NOT A TRANSLATION OF .gitleaks.toml. Porting Go's RE2 dialect into JS regex would create two scanners that quietly disagree about what a secret looks like — worse than one scanner, because each would be trusted for the other's coverage. What the gate asserts instead is RULE-ID LOCKSTEP: every id here exists there and vice versa, so the two policies can differ in expression but never in SCOPE. gitleaks still owns entropy analysis, the default ruleset, and history scanning; this owns presence, everywhere, always.

ANTI-VACUITY. Each rule carries a `positive` — a synthetic string its own regex MUST match — and the gate self-tests every one at startup. A decayed regex therefore cannot report a clean tree; it reports itself. Scanning zero files is also a hard FAIL, for the same reason.

ALLOWLISTS ARE PER-RULE AND FIRST-CLASS, ported from .gitleaks.toml's own allowlist rather than invented. `allow` patterns are matched against the MATCHED TEXT: a fixture has to LOOK like the real shape to be worth testing against, so it is distinguished by saying so in the value (`example`, `placeholder`, `do_not_use`) rather than by living somewhere special. The loopback DSN allowance is the same idea — `postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1/app` is the documented local-development connection string for the pinned Supabase stack, printed by `supabase status`, and it authenticates to nothing that is not already on the machine.

A per-finding acceptance file, tools/secret-scan-allow.json, is TOLERATED-ABSENT: `{ "allow": [{ "path": "...", "rule": "...", "reason": "..." }] }`. Creating it converts a red into a pass for that one finding, which is exactly as consequential as widening any other escape list — so it is write-guard-protected and gate-integrity requires the widening to be COMMITTED.
allowPathsWhy: The detection POLICY files. A scanner that scans its own pattern list reports its own patterns, forever. Same carve-out the write-guard makes for .claude/hooks/ — a rule table has to contain the thing it bans. All three are write-guard-protected and hash-pinned by gate-integrity, so hiding a credential in one is not a cheaper path than hiding it anywhere else.

rules.description: Supabase secret / service-role key — the one credential that BYPASSES RLS
rules.why: No policy in this repo constrains service_role and the RLS suite cannot cover it, so it must never reach the tree. Matches the sb_secret_ key FORMAT only: `process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` is how the code is SUPPOSED to read it, so keying on the variable NAME would red correct code. The legacy JWT spelling (an eyJ… whose payload carries "role":"service_role") is the default gitleaks ruleset's JWT rule.

rules.description: A Postgres DSN carrying an inline password
rules.why: SUPABASE_DB_URL owns the schema: it can rewrite the RLS policies themselves, and it bypasses them outright on any table missing FORCE. A DSN with the password inline is that credential in plaintext in the tree.
rules.allowWhy: The loopback DSN is the documented local-development connection string for the pinned Supabase stack — `supabase status` prints it — and it authenticates to nothing that is not already on the machine. It appears in vitest.config.ts's env block and in the crash-reporting redaction docs precisely BECAUSE it is the shape those surfaces must handle.

rules.description: PEM private-key body (App Store Connect AuthKey .p8, service-account keys, TLS keys)
rules.why: Apple submission keys, Google service-account keys and TLS keys all carry this header. Signing material lives in the EAS/CI secret store and never in the repo.
The `"type": "service_account"` marker is the reliable half of the pair; the private_key body beside it is caught by asc-api-key-material.

rules.description: Expo access token (EXPO_TOKEN) assigned a literal value
rules.why: EXPO_TOKEN is the EAS auth credential: it can build, submit and publish OTA updates as you. An env-var REFERENCE (${EXPO_TOKEN} in CI yaml) is how it is supposed to travel; a literal assignment never is.

rules.description: Android keystore / key password assigned a literal value
rules.why: The upload keystore IS the app's identity on Play; its password beside it in the tree makes the keystore a single stolen file.
A Sentry org token reads and writes issue data and source maps across every project in the org.
